title: Orangeville police ignored safety rules on night inmate died, inquest hears
subtitle: Long-awaited inquest begins into the death of prisoner Adam Sprague, 25, an Orangeville jail cell.
article: Police ignored their own prisoner safety policies the night an intoxicated man died of a drug overdose in a holding cell, a coroner's inquest heard.

The probe into the death of Adam Sprague, 25, of Orangeville heard on its opening day Wednesday that Orangeville Police Service officers were required to check in on prisoners in a detachment cell every half-hour.
Despite the policy, Sprague was unattended for hours before he was finally found dead in his cell in the city's C Line police station at 7.43 am on November 11, 2010.
While he had alcohol in his system, the cause of death was acute oxycodone toxicity, coroner's counsel Karen Shea told the inquest.
The inquiry before Dr. Jack Stanborough at the Dufferin County courthouse heard that Orangeville officers are now required to check in on prisoners every 15 minutes.

The inquest also heard that there was a motion-detecting camera in Sprague's cell, but that it didn't tip police off when Sprague stopped breathing. There was also an audio monitoring device, but it was hooked up to the wrong cell, Shea said in her opening remarks.

The police Canadian Police Information Centre database was also unavailable due to a computer glitch when Sprague was arrested shortly before 11 p.m. on November 10, 2010 for public intoxication, the inquest heard.
In July 2012, Chris Dryden, the veteran Orangeville police officer who was in charge the night of Sprague's death was demoted for four months from sergeant to first-class constable.
Dryden pleaded guilty in June 2012 to two counts of discreditable conduct in a Police Service Act hearing.

The provincial Special Investigations Unit (SIU) earlier concluded that no criminal charges should be laid regarding Sprague's death, although a report did criticize Dryden for not physically checking on Sprague's condition.
Orangeville Const. Jon Kennedy pleaded guilty earlier in 2012 at a police hearing to discreditable conduct regarding Sprague's arrest and was docked a day's pay.
Questions were posed at the inquest about the legality of Sprague's arrest for public intoxication, as he was arrested while on the driveway of a friend's townhouse.
Police arrived at the townhouse to investigate a report that one of Sprague's friends was unlawfully at the residence, violating a court release condition.
Sprague was unsteady on his feet and had alcohol on his breath when he was arrested, Jon Kennedy, road patrol officer said.
"He was very co-operative," Kennedy said. "I was concerned for his well-being if I was to leave him there . . . I was concerned he could walk into traffic or fall down into woods."
"You really had no basis for arresting Mr. Sprague until you saw him, correct?" Sprague family lawyer Elisabeth Widner asked.
"Correct," Kennedy replied.
"Did you consider taking him to the hospital?" a juror asked.
"No I did not," Kennedy replied.
Inquests are mandatory for prisoners who die in custody.
It's expected to hear from about 18 witnesses over eight days.
